description: I'm an engineering student passionate about AI, Python, data science, and web development. Our project, EarthTrace AI, aims to build an interactive global climate analysis platform using NASA Earth observation data. It will visualize environmental trends, analyze historical changes, and test statistical significance. I'm looking for enthusiastic teammates skilled in React, UI/UX design, Python, GIS, climate science, and data analytics to build an innovative, impactful solution.
summary: EarthTrace AI helps people investigate how Earth’s climate is changing using NASA data. Its interactive map displays annual temperature anomalies from NASA GISTEMP, while regional charts show long-term trends and statistical uncertainty. Users can compare geographic areas, explore temperature and rainfall for a selected location through NASA POWER, and view natural events from NASA EONET for context. Weather forecasts and climate-model outlooks appear separately from historical observations, so future estimates are clearly identified. The app also lets users export data and a scientific PDF, making its findings easier to review and share
details:
EarthTrace AI is an interactive climate-trend explorer created by Team OrbitX for the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. It helps users move from a global view of change to a testable conclusion about a chosen region. The app turns NASA GISTEMP v4 temperature-anomaly data into annual maps and area-weighted regional time series. It reports a trend per decade, confidence interval and significance result, with additional statistical checks. Users can compare two regions and export observations as CSV or a scientific PDF.

For a selected location, EarthTrace AI retrieves NASA POWER temperature and precipitation estimates. NASA EONET event markers add geographic context; they are not treated as proof of a climate trend or its cause. Separate Open-Meteo views show weather forecasts and climate-model outlooks, clearly distinguished from historical NASA analyses.

We intend to make Earth-system evidence easier for students, educators and the public to explore and question. We built the app in Python using Streamlit, xarray, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels and Plotly, with MapLibre GL JS for the browser globe. It needs no special hardware. We considered missing data, geographic coverage, uncertainty, service outages and the risk of mistaking projections for observations. The app explains these limits rather than inventing missing values.
